paragraphs: Ice on the Tennis Court, posted by Lily. Last month, the Explorers took a short chemistry course at the science museum. The Explorers like chemistry, because every lesson has a surprise. Guide Ann was our teacher, and the course had three lessons. At the end, she gave us an experiment to do at school. We did it on the school tennis court on a sunny Thursday. We wore hats, and we drank a lot of water.

Water freezes at zero degrees, and ice melts at zero degrees. The ice in a freezer is much colder, at about minus eighteen degrees. In our town, the air is warm, so ice melts fast. You can see this in a cold drink with ice. The temperature on the tennis court was thirty-five degrees. That is hot enough for a good test.

We made three kinds of ice cubes: normal ice, ice with salt, and ice with sugar. The cubes came from the school kitchen. We put one cube of each kind on the court in a line. We also had one extra cube of each kind, in case a cube fell. Mia started the clock, and Leo watched the cubes. May wrote the times in a table. Mia took a photo of the cubes every ten minutes. The photos are on the blog, and you can look at them.

The normal cube melted in forty minutes. The sugar cube melted in thirty minutes. The salt cube melted in twenty minutes. Leo shouted, "The salt cube is first!" The total time for the three cubes was ninety minutes. The salt cube was the fastest.

Guide Ann explained the answer with a simple fact. Salt makes water freeze at a lower temperature, so ice with salt melts faster. The cold water and the salt mix, and the ice melts faster. Sugar does the same job, but it is slower. In very cold places, people put salt on the roads, because it melts the ice. A scientist can use this fact to keep roads safe in winter.

Our test was not perfect, because the cubes were not exactly the same size. However, the answer agrees with the facts of the course. Next time, Leo wants to test ice with lemon juice. Do you want to try it at home with an adult? Tell us the answer in a message!
